title: POC Weekly Sync - Dedicated Sizing & Autoscale Planning
summary: Weekly POC sync to review pilot results, discuss Dedicated sizing for production, autoscaling policy options, and burst capacity planning. Action items: run targeted burst load test, share Dedicated cost estimate and a recommended autoscale configuration, follow up with kernel-level perf run and security checklist. Customer leaning toward Dedicated but wants clear latency SLOs and predictable cost under spiky traffic.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (Nimbus Head of ML), Tom Reeves (Nimbus Infra Eng), Priya Shah (Nimbus Eng Manager)

Summary (auto): rough: reviewing pilot perf numbers, discuss Dedicated sizing, autoscale rules and burst.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check in — can you hear me OK?
[00:05] Alicia Gomez: yes loud and clear, thanks Maya, we've pulled the latest dashboard so we can walk through the numbers.
[00:12] Samir Patel: great, i'll share my screen - i'll start with the p50/p95 numbers from the pilot cluster, note that these are from the hosted pilot with prefix caching enabled.
[00:20] Tom Reeves: one quick thing, the traffic we ran yesterday included a few 200-user bursts from our staging load generator, hope that's visible in the logs.
[00:28] Samir Patel: yep i can see that, ok so baseline: average QPS ~35, sustained 10min windows peaked at 120 qps during test, p50 token latency ~70ms, p95 ~420ms for 1k token requests with small batch sizes (2-4).
[00:40] Priya Shah: those p95 spikes are the worry — in prod we'll have more bursty patient lookup queries where latency matters.
[00:46] Maya Chen: understood, main question today is how Dedicated sizing and autoscale should be configured to hit your latency SLOs while controlling cost. also planning for burst capacity and how we handle fallback to smaller models if capacity constrained.
[00:55] Alicia Gomez: high level constraint: we need p95 < 500ms for the critical route, and cost per 1k reqs needs to stay within our forecast; timeline to decide in two weeks for procurement.
[01:10] Samir Patel: OK, recommended approach: start Dedicated with 2 reserved GPU nodes (A100 equivalent), configure autoscale with a min of 2 and max of 6, with surge/burst pool that can borrow spare capacity for short windows. autoscale triggers: CPU/gpu utilization + queue length + latency percentiles.
[01:30] Tom Reeves: can you explain burst pool? is that billed differently or throttled?
[01:36] Samir Patel: burst pool is essentially unreserved capacity that we can route to when the reserved pool is saturated; it is billed at on-demand rates and there's a routing policy to prefer reserved nodes first. we can set a hard cap on burst to limit cost exposure.
[01:50] Priya Shah: how fast does autoscale spin up additional nodes? our spikes are short — 30-90s — spinning GPUs in that window sounds risky.
[01:58] Maya Chen: good point. for very short bursts we recommend request queuing + prefix/KV cache warm-up + aggressive batching where possible; for mid-length bursts (2-10 min) we can use pre-warmed burst nodes or a small warm pool kept ready, which costs more but avoids spin-up latency.
[02:15] Alicia Gomez: what about model variants, e.g., a quantized 4-bit variant for non-critical routes? can we fallback automatically?
[02:22] Samir Patel: yes we have automatic fallback policies — route by policy: if latency SLO violated or queue length > threshold then fallback to quantized model variant or shorter context model. we've observed ~1.5-2x token cost reduction with 4-bit quantization with modest quality delta on our evals.
[02:40] Tom Reeves: curious about tail latency — you mentioned the p95 spikes coincide with cache misses?
[02:45] Samir Patel: exactly. p95 correlates with KV cache cold starts and large batch alignment issues. tuning TTLs and pre-warming the KV cache for top prefixes reduced p95 by ~30% in our internal tests.
[02:58] Priya Shah: ok so next step from technical side: we'll need a plan for warm pool sizing and cache priming. how do we estimate warm pool size?
[03:07] Samir Patel: formula: target burst headroom = peak QPS - reserved capacity throughput. capacity per worker depends on model and sequence length; from your pilot, one A100-equivalent node handles ~60 sustained QPS at p50 latency for your average payload. so with min=2 reserved nodes = ~120 QPS baseline; your 120 qps peak yesterday used up baseline so you'd need additional warm nodes only for larger spikes.
[03:30] Alicia Gomez: so two nodes baseline, if we want to cover 200 qps peak without falling back we'd need ~4 nodes?
[03:36] Samir Patel: roughly yes — 200/60 ≈ 3.3 -> round to 4. but if you rely on autoscale with 2 min spin time you might still see tail spikes, so warm pool of 1-2 nodes looks prudent.
[03:50] Maya Chen: cost tradeoff — keeping 1 warm node reserved costs X per hour, burst on-demand costs Y per hour; we'll send a cost comparison.
[03:58] Tom Reeves: please include an example run-rate for 30-min daily burst vs continuous. helps procurement.
[04:05] Priya Shah: if we go with the fallback model route, how do we measure quality delta? we have clinical NLP tasks so quality matters.
[04:12] Samir Patel: we'll run a small eval set you provide and benchmark the quantized variant vs full precision on your prompts. we can also set canary rules so only a slice of traffic is routed to fallback and measure user-visible metrics.
[04:24] Alicia Gomez: security question: with Dedicated, how does KMS/HSM integration and audit logging look? any SOC2 gap?
[04:30] Maya Chen: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS for key encryption and we can forward audit logs to your SIEM. Redwood has SOC2 and we provide evidence in our security pack; we'll attach the security checklist and the dedicated deployment guide.
[04:44] Tom Reeves: network topology — we need VPC peering and private endpoint access; will that affect autoscale latency at all?
[04:50] Samir Patel: minimal; peering adds a few ms at most. spin-up time for nodes is independent of networking. the biggest is instance provisioning and model load time.
[04:58] Maya Chen: let's capture concrete action items now.
[05:02] Alicia Gomez: great.
[05:05] [05:05] Maya Chen: Action item 1: Redwood (Samir) to run a kernel-level perf with your 1k token workload and share a throughput map, due by 2025-02-18.
[05:14] [05:14] Samir Patel: noted. i'll coordinate with infra to run the perf and include batch size sensitivity.
[05:19] [05:19] Maya Chen: Action item 2: Redwood (Maya) to send Dedicated cost breakdown for a 2->6 autoscale config plus warm pool scenarios and 30-min daily burst examples, due 2025-02-14.
[05:29] [05:29] Maya Chen: Action item 3: Nimbus (Alicia/Tom) to provide a 200-sample eval set for quantized model quality checks and clarify critical routes, due 2025-02-17.
[05:40] [05:40] Priya Shah: Action item 4: Nimbus (Tom) to run an internal 90s burst test with trace IDs and share logs so we can correlate p95 spikes, due 2025-02-16.
[05:52] Maya Chen: Sound good, any other blockers?
[05:55] Alicia Gomez: procurement timeline — two weeks to sign off but we need the cost sheet.
[05:59] Tom Reeves: also would like recommended autoscale policy JSON snippet for our infra team to review.
[06:05] Samir Patel: we'll include a sample policy and recommended thresholds.
[06:10] Maya Chen: ok wrapping — we'll follow up via email, samir will post results to the shared drive, maya will attach security pack and cost estimate, nimbus will run the tests. thanks everyone.
[06:20] Alicia Gomez: thanks all. bye.

Notes: transcription contains occasional filler and minor mishears (e.g., 'queue' transcribed as 'cue' in some timestamps).
